lesson.title: How Fast Can the Output Actually Move
lesson.summary: Slew rate is the maximum rate of change a real op-amp's output can produce, and when a signal demands a faster ramp than that limit, the output distorts into a ramp or triangle regardless of what the ideal gain equation predicts.
lesson.body:
Bandwidth, from the previous chapter, describes a small-signal limitation: how the op-amp's gain falls off with frequency for signals that stay small. Slew rate is a different and separate limit, one that shows up on large output swings. Internally, the op-amp has to charge and discharge a compensation capacitor to move its output, and the internal stages driving that capacitor can only supply a limited current. That limited current, divided by the capacitance, caps how many volts per second the output can physically change by, no matter how the feedback network is configured. Datasheets list this cap directly as slew rate, in volts per microsecond (V/µs).

For a sine wave, the rate of change is fastest at the zero crossing, not at the peak. For an output of peak amplitude Vp and frequency f, that maximum rate of change works out to 2π f Vp. Setting this equal to the op-amp's rated slew rate SR and solving for frequency gives the largest frequency at which a full-amplitude sine wave can still be reproduced without distortion: f_max = SR / (2π Vp). Above f_max at that amplitude, the op-amp physically cannot keep up with the sine wave's steepest slope.

Here is a worked example. Take an op-amp with SR = 0.5 V/µs, typical of an older general-purpose part, driving a sine wave with a 5 V peak (10 V peak-to-peak). Converting SR to volts per second gives 0.5 x 10^6 V/s, or 500,000 V/s. Then f_max = 500,000 / (2π x 5) = 500,000 / 31.416 = 15,915 Hz, or about 15.9 kHz. Push the output past roughly 16 kHz at that amplitude and the sine wave stops looking like a sine wave.

A second version of the same check makes a good design habit: instead of solving for the maximum frequency, verify a specific design point directly. Suppose a circuit is meant to output a 5 V peak sine wave at 20 kHz. The slope it demands at the zero crossing is 2π x 20,000 x 5 = 628,318 V/s, which is 0.628 V/µs. Compare that against the op-amp's rated 0.5 V/µs: the design asks for more slope than the part can deliver, so the output will visibly flatten into a rounded, almost triangular shape at its steepest points instead of tracing a clean sine. Fixing it means choosing a faster op-amp, lowering the amplitude, or lowering the frequency.

It's worth keeping bandwidth and slew rate mentally separate even though both limit high-frequency performance. An op-amp can have generous GBW and still slew-limit badly on a large swing, because slew rate is set by internal bias currents charging a capacitor, a completely different mechanism from the small-signal gain rolloff that GBW describes. A thorough design check tests both: does the closed-loop bandwidth cover the signal's frequency content, and separately, does the required dV/dt at the signal's actual amplitude stay under the rated slew rate.
